label: Apply iterative refinement techniques for progressive improvement
model: claude-opus-5 (authored in a Claude Code session)

cards.front: What is the mental model for iterative refinement, and what part of the loop carries the most value?
cards.back: Gradient descent: start at a rough approximation, measure the distance from your target, adjust, repeat. The FEEDBACK — the measurement — is more valuable than the initial output. The goal is to converge together, not to get it right once.

cards.front: Name the five core refinement techniques.
cards.back: 1) Progressive improvement — ask for a rough first pass. 2) Input/output examples as a refinement anchor. 3) Test-driven iteration — give the failing tests first. 4) The interview pattern — clarify before implementing. 5) Structured feedback loops — name exactly what was wrong and what should change.

cards.front: Why explicitly frame the first request as a rough draft?
cards.back: 'Give me a rough first pass at this function. We'll refine it.' shifts the interaction from 'get it right once' to 'converge together', lowers the model's tendency to over-hedge and over-explain, and gives you a concrete artifact to react to instead of a blank page.

cards.front: Why are input/output examples better than an abstract description of behaviour?
cards.back: Abstract descriptions are ambiguous; concrete input → output pairs are not. They act as the prompting equivalent of a unit-test suite — each example, especially an edge case, rules out a class of incorrect implementations and gives Claude an objective test to reason against while generating.

cards.front: How does the TDD cycle map onto prompt refinement?
cards.back: RED — provide the failing test cases as part of the prompt. GREEN — ask for the implementation that satisfies them. REFACTOR/IMPROVE — review and request cleanup. If a test fails, feed the failure back verbatim (assertion plus received value) so Claude can reason about the exact mismatch.

cards.front: What is the interview pattern, and what does it save?
cards.back: Instruct Claude to identify ambiguities and ask clarifying questions BEFORE writing code — 'only proceed once you have enough information.' One well-structured clarification round often halves the number of revision cycles, and it's most valuable when constraints are non-obvious (performance budgets, data shape assumptions, side-effect boundaries).

cards.front: What makes feedback 'structured', and why does it matter?
cards.back: It names what the output did, what you expected, and the difference — e.g. 'The previous version creates a new array on every call. Refactor to reuse the existing buffer.' Vague feedback like 'make it better' produces vague improvements; precise feedback produces targeted corrections.

cards.front: Exam trap: should you restate the full specification on every refinement turn?
cards.back: No. Claude retains the conversation, so refer to the previous output by reference ('in the previous version'). Restating everything wastes context and introduces inconsistencies between turns.

cards.front: A test fails on the first implementation. What's the wrong reflex, and the right move?
cards.back: Wrong: discarding the implementation and rewriting from scratch. A single failing test usually indicates a localised defect — paste the exact failure back and ask for the targeted fix, which preserves the parts that already work.

cards.front: What does 'closing the loop' mean after a correction, and why is it needed?
cards.back: Re-verify the corrected implementation against ALL prior examples and tests, not just the one that failed — otherwise the fix can silently regress behaviour an earlier example already pinned down. Also avoid the opposite error at the start: don't overload the first prompt with every edge case, which produces bloated, defensive output. Lead with the core case and layer edge cases in during refinement.
